title: Don't seek the true
hook: the poem: don't seek the true, just stop holding opinions

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hair's breadth: the smallest lean of liking and disliking, and heaven and earth set apart. Did you catch one bias while it was still only a flicker? Day one thousand two hundred fourteen.

How many opinions have you held since you woke up? About the weather. The traffic. Someone's haircut, a headline, the way the coffee came out. Plenty of them nobody asked for, and plenty are gone by lunch. They arrive on their own, like notifications. Now here is a poem, a religious poem, chanted in some Chan and Zen halls, and in the middle of it comes a line that sounds almost backwards. You might expect it to say: seek the truth with all your heart. It says the opposite. Today: don't seek the true.
screen: `OPINIONS SINCE BREAKFAST.` → `A RELIGIOUS POEM.` → `A LINE THAT SOUNDS BACKWARDS.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In paraphrase, the Xinxin Ming says: do not seek the true; just stop holding opinions. It is a startling thing to put in a poem about the way. Isn't truth the point? Second, look at the word just. The poem isn't saying truth doesn't matter. It is saying that hunting for it, as if it were a prize somewhere else, is one more kind of grabbing, one more round of picking and choosing. The poem has already said the way is round and complete, like vast space, with nothing lacking. So the instruction is not go and find it. The instruction is stop doing the thing that covers it. Third, holding versus having. Opinions will keep arriving; the line doesn't ask you to stop thinking. It asks you to stop clutching. An opinion you can set down is a thought. An opinion you can't set down has become a wall, and you end up seeing the wall instead of the person, the movie, the rainy afternoon. Yesterday's hair's breadth was the first lean. An opinion is that lean after it has set hard. Fourth, what's left when you put one down. Not emptiness. The thing itself, unedited. The coworker, before your verdict on her. The song, before you decided it was overplayed. The poem's wager is that this, the plain thing without your commentary, is closer to what you were seeking in the first place. The line makes that wager in a handful of words.
screen: `THE LINE: DON'T SEEK THE TRUE.` · `THE KEY WORD IS 'JUST'.` · `HOLDING, NOT HAVING.` · `THE THING ITSELF, UNEDITED.` · then, large: `JUST STOP HOLDING OPINIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like to try it. Sit and let the breath come and go on its own. Within a few breaths, a comment will show up about the sitting itself. This is going well. I'm bad at this. My knee. Those are opinions too. Each time one comes, see it, and set it down, the way you'd set a cup on a table. You don't have to argue with it. Then, before the bell, choose one topic you'll hold no opinion about for an hour today: the weather, the news, someone's outfit. The bell holds the time.
Don't seek the true. The Xinxin Ming's line that turns the search around: don't hunt for truth somewhere else, just stop holding opinions. Today's word.
Your line: just stop holding opinions. Pick one topic and, for one hour today, let it go without a verdict. Day one thousand two hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: In Zen and Chan practice this line is sometimes quoted in talks and used during sitting as a reminder to let commentary about the sitting, and about everything else, go by without holding on to it.

fork.setup: a friend asks your take on a show you half-watched. today's line comes to mind. what fits it best?
options: say you don't have one, and ask what they saw
argue the opposite to keep things lively
fork.reveal: the poem doesn't forbid speaking. it asks you to stop gripping views, and having no take leaves room for the show, and your friend, as they are.

original.note: Chinese (xi jian): 'stop views', the poem's 'just stop holding opinions'.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't seek the true means truth doesn't matter.
what it means: stop hunting for truth as a prize elsewhere; just stop holding opinions, and what was sought is already here.
what a scholar hears: the verb for 'stop', 息, also means to rest, so some readers hear the line as letting views come to rest rather than fighting them off.

sources.ref: Xinxin Ming, the line on not seeking the true and ceasing views
sources.work: Xinxin Ming (Faith in Mind), attributed to Sengcan

notes: The line is paraphrased; nothing quoted.
Check the original wording (commonly 不用求真，唯須息見) and the gloss of 息見 (xi jian) as 'stop views'; pronunciation approximates Mandarin xī jiàn.
Trapdoor: 息 as 'cease' and 'rest' is a dictionary sense; the reading 'letting views come to rest' is attributed to 'some readers'. Keeper to confirm or cut.
'The way is round and complete, like vast space, with nothing lacking' refers to 圓同太虛，無欠無餘 (paraphrased on day 1212); an earlier draft said 'not hidden', which is not a line of the poem.

Editor pass: replaced 'the poem has told us the way is not hidden' (not a line of the poem) with its actual image, round and complete like vast space; softened 'most' claims about the listener and 'carried and chanted in Chan and Zen halls' to 'some'; cut the stock 'Chan teachers have pointed at that wager in many ways'.
